project.title: The Company That Sells You Nothing

1.question: How can a gym support this many members?
1.reveal: The empty room is the contradiction: huge membership, limited physical capacity.
1.hook: THE COMPANY THAT SELLS YOU NOTHING

2.question: What if low attendance is not a failure?
2.reveal: The business model benefits when members do not consume scarce capacity.

3.question: Why would friction be the product?
3.reveal: The story moves from fitness to recurring-payment psychology.

4.question: How does a payment become background noise?
4.reveal: $86 becomes $219 when consumers itemize; $133 is the perceptual gap.

5.question: Where did the pattern spread?
5.reveal: The mechanism is portable across industries.

6.question: What kind of member creates the best economics?
6.reveal: Capacity is the scarce resource; usage changes marginal service cost.

7.question: What is this revenue called?
7.reveal: Human intention and non-use become part of the economics.

8.question: How is subscription breakage different from a gift card?
8.reveal: The mechanism gets a name: BREAKAGE.

9.question: What does recurring forgetting become?
9.reveal: A one-time break becomes a recurring stream of revenue.

10.question: If this works, why did older gyms use hard contracts?
10.reveal: The weakness of the model becomes the next story problem.

11.question: Why did the contract become a liability?
11.reveal: A visible contract creates a visible dispute and an identifiable complaint.

12.question: What replaces the visible contract?
12.reveal: The visible weapon disappears; friction becomes the replacement.

13.question: Can a low price make leaving feel irrational?
13.reveal: Low price plus friction can replace long contracts.

14.question: Why can stopping feel more expensive than continuing?
14.reveal: Time and attention become hidden cancellation costs.

15.question: What happens when software applies the same model to ownership?
15.reveal: The gym is selling an intention gap, not only access.

16.question: What happens when a one-time purchase becomes a recurring relationship?
16.reveal: The subscription idea migrates from gym access into owned software.

17.question: Why is one-time ownership a problem for Adobe?
17.reveal: A product can remain excellent while the upgrade cycle leaves revenue waiting.

18.question: What if the product itself stops being a one-time purchase?
18.reveal: Creative Suite ends; Creative Cloud becomes the continuing relationship.

19.question: How did customers react to ownership being replaced?
19.reveal: The backlash is evidence that the economic relationship changed for the customer too.

20.question: Did the subscription model actually change the economics?
20.reveal: Adobe subscription revenue grows from the historical 2013 base to much larger modern recurring revenue.

21.question: Where else did the model spread?
21.reveal: Streaming provides a larger consumer proof point.

22.question: Why did streaming feel like an escape from cable?
22.reveal: The original promise was pay-for-what-you-want flexibility.

23.question: What happens when every studio wants its own relationship with the customer?
23.reveal: The catalogue fragments and more subscription decisions appear.

24.question: Did streaming rebuild the bundle?
24.reveal: Many small recurring charges recreate the logic of one large recurring bill.

25.question: What matters most once the subscription is easy to start?
25.reveal: The exit becomes the most revealing part of the system.

26.question: What did regulators allege about the entrance to Prime?
26.reveal: The investigation moves from business economics into interface behavior.

27.question: What happens when cancellation is designed as a sequence instead of a button?
27.reveal: Each retention step increases the effort required to leave.

28.question: What did insiders call the cancellation sequence?
28.reveal: Iliad — an understated but powerful name for a long cancellation journey.

29.question: How consequential did the case become?

30.question: Was Amazon unique?
30.reveal: Adobe faces a separate cancellation case; the mechanism appears across industries.

31.question: Would a federal rule finally solve the exit problem?
31.reveal: Click-to-Cancel promises symmetry between entry and exit.

32.question: What happens to the fix when it is challenged?
32.reveal: The federal rule is vacated before enforcement begins.

33.question: Why did the rule fail?
33.reveal: The court's ruling turns on regulatory procedure, not an endorsement of deceptive design.

34.question: What is the legal situation now?
34.reveal: No nationwide federal Click-to-Cancel rule is currently in force; other laws may still apply.

35.question: Why does the empty gym still matter?
35.reveal: The economics are not only about fitness; they are about attention and inertia.

36.question: What did the opening image actually mean?
36.reveal: The empty gym is no longer a mystery; it is evidence of the business logic.

37.question: What link did subscriptions weaken?
37.reveal: Payment can continue after active consumption stops.

38.question: What should the $133 figure actually mean?
38.reveal: It is a measured perception gap, not a claim that everyone wastes exactly $133.

39.question: What can the viewer do right now?
39.reveal: Audit twelve months of recurring charges and turn silent renewals back into explicit choices.

40.question: What is the real choice underneath the whole story?
40.reveal: A subscription should remain a deliberate choice, not an unnoticed agreement that keeps running.
40.loop: Return to the empty-gym motif so the final frame can conceptually rhyme with the opening.
